a: The steady bearing — risk of collision exists
o: The AIS — its CPA comes from her own GNSS
The AIS — 1.8 M is a safe passing distance
Neither — call her and agree how to pass
why: Rule 7(a), (d)(i): a steady compass bearing means risk, and if in doubt risk is deemed to exist — AIS is one means, not the judge.

fig.title: Night, 2200, clear
lines: AIS: ship A, CPA 1.8 M, TCPA 14 min
Radar: her compass bearing steady
for 10 minutes, range closing

q: Your mate says her bearing has drawn 20° left since the turn, so she will pass clear. Will she?
a: No — her compass bearing is still 040°T
o: Yes — a 20° change of bearing is plenty
Yes — once her bearing moves, risk is gone
No — but only because she is now inside 3 M
why: Rule 7(d)(i): judge by compass bearing — 020°T + 20° relative = 040°T, unchanged: risk still exists, and your turn was too small.

fig.title: Night, under power
lines: 2300: you 000°T, ship 040° relative
2302: you come 20° to starboard
2310: you 020°T, ship 020° relative
Range 4.0 M, now 2.6 M

q: Your 23 m motor yacht is about to cross this dredged channel. A deep-draught ship coming down it bears steady on your port bow. What do you do?
a: Wait — do not cross if it would impede her
o: Hold on — she has you on her starboard side
Cross now — only boats under 20 m must wait
Cross now, sounding five short to warn her
why: Rule 9(d): no vessel of any size may cross a narrow channel if that impedes one that can navigate only within it — 9(b)'s 20 m limit isn't here.

fig.note: Dredged channel · ship 1.5 M, bearing steady

q: Your 22 m motor yacht is bound for Port A, inside this inshore traffic zone. May you leave the lane and use the zone to get there?
a: Yes — you are bound for a port within the zone
o: No — at 22 m under power you must stay in the lane
Only under sail — power must keep to the lane
Only by day — at night you must use the lane
why: Rule 10(d)(ii): any vessel may use an inshore traffic zone when en route to or from a port, installation or place situated within it.

fig.note: Traffic separation scheme · north up

q: You must cross this scheme to the north under sail, but the wind blows straight down the right-angle heading. What do you do?
a: Motor-sail across on a heading of 000°T
o: Sail across close-hauled on 045°T
Tack across in short boards up the lanes
Wait in the separation zone for a shift
why: Rule 10(c): cross on a heading as nearly as practicable at right angles to the flow — with an engine aboard, 000°T is practicable.

fig.note: Traffic separation scheme · north up

q: You are sailing east along this lane at night in your 22 m sloop. Where in the lane do you keep?
a: Near its outer edge, well clear of the zone
o: Close along the edge of the separation zone
Inside the separation zone, out of the way
Down the middle, where the ships expect you
why: Rule 10(b)(ii): keep clear of a separation line or zone; near the outer edge you also impede the ships least (10(j)).

fig.note: Traffic separation scheme · north up

q: Your 22 m motor yacht is joining the eastbound lane from its side, at the small angle Rule 10 asks for. This ship in the lane is closing on your port quarter, bearing steady. Who keeps clear?
a: She does — she is overtaking you
o: You do — a vessel joining gives way to the lane
You do — she is the larger, less handy vessel
Neither — Rule 10 replaces the steering rules
why: She is 150° from your bow, over 22.5° abaft your beam, seeing your sternlight: Rule 13 — she keeps clear; 10(a) keeps every other Rule in force.

fig.note: Night · joining the lane at 15° · you 10 kn, she 16 kn

q: You must stop to change the impeller. Where may you do it?
a: In the separation zone — an emergency allows it
o: In the lane, showing NUC lights while you work
At anchor near the end of the scheme
Anywhere — once stopped, Rule 10 stops applying
why: Rule 10(e)(i): a separation zone may be entered in an emergency to avoid immediate danger; 10(g) bars anchoring near a scheme's ends.

fig.title: 0230, crossing a scheme
lines: Your 22 m motor yacht, one engine
Overheating: 20 min left at low revs
You are in the eastbound lane
Separation zone 4 cables north

q: Crossing a lane under sail in your 22 m ketch, you see these lights on your port bow. Who keeps clear?
a: You — avoid impeding her: she's constrained by draught
o: She does — power keeps clear of sail
She does — she has you on her starboard side
Neither — three reds mean she is aground
why: Rules 18(d) and 28: three all-round reds mark a CBD vessel — all but NUC and RAM avoid impeding her, as 10(j) also asks of you.

fig.note: Night · crossing the lane · on your port bow, steady

q: Which of you must avoid impeding the tanker?
a: Both — the trawler as well as you
o: Only you — a fishing vessel is exempt
Only the trawler — you are under sail
Neither — in a lane Rule 10 replaces 18
why: Rule 18(d)(i): every vessel but NUC and RAM avoids impeding a CBD vessel — fishing included; in a lane 10(i) and 10(j) say it again.

fig.title: Westbound lane, clear night
lines: Tanker: in the lane, CBD lights
Trawler: trawling across her bow
You: 23 m sloop under sail, close by

q: Close-hauled at night, you see this yacht's masthead tricolour showing red, the bearing steady. Who keeps clear?
a: You — you cannot tell which tack she is on
o: She does — she is the yacht to windward
She does — her red shows she is on port tack
Neither — both of you bear away to starboard
why: Her red puts her heading between 150° and 262°T — either tack in a north wind; Rule 12(a)(iii): on port tack, you keep clear.

fig.note: Wind N · you 045°T, port tack · she bears 330°T

q: Your 24 m motor yacht is overtaking this sailing yacht on her port side. Your harbour lies to the east. When may you turn across her bow?
a: Only when finally past and clear, well ahead
o: As soon as you are abeam of her
Now — she must hold her course and speed
Once ahead — then she must keep clear of you
why: Rule 13(d): a later change of bearing doesn't make you a crossing vessel — keep clear until finally past and clear; Rule 18 says the same.

fig.note: You 24 kn · she 6 kn · your harbour lies east

q: Your 22 m motor yacht at 15 kn and this ship at 15 kn are closing almost end-on. What do you do?
a: A bold turn to starboard, early — pass port to port
o: A small turn to port to open the green-to-green pass
Hold on — green to green, she will pass you clear
A small turn to starboard, then watch her CPA
why: Rule 14(c): in doubt, assume head-on and turn to starboard, boldly — a small turn cuts the 0.3 M CPA, and a port turn can cancel hers.

fig.note: 6 M, 3° to starboard · AIS CPA 0.3 M, stbd to stbd

q: What do the Rules ask of you with these two ships?
a: Keep clear of B, boldly — and keep watching A
o: Hold on — A gives way to you, so you stand on
Turn to port to pass astern of A, clear of B
Wait for A to act first, then deal with B
why: Rule 15: B has you on her port side — keep clear of her (16); you remain stand-on for A, so watch her under Rule 17 as you turn.

lines: You: 23 m motor yacht, 000°T, 12 kn
A: ship 40° on your port bow, 3 M
B: ship 40° on your stbd bow, 3 M
Both bearings steady; neither alters

q: Your 22 m motor yacht is the stand-on vessel. When may you first act on your own to avoid this ship?
a: Now — it is apparent she is not keeping clear
o: Only when she is too close to avoid you alone
Never — the stand-on vessel holds on to the end
Only once she has answered your five short
why: Rule 17(a)(ii): you may act as soon as it is apparent she is not taking appropriate action; 17(b) makes it a duty only at the last stage.

fig.title: Clear night, you stand on
lines: Ship on your port bow, bearing 300°T
0310: no reply to your five short
0312: 3.0 M, bearing still 300°T

q: You are the stand-on vessel in your 22 m motor yacht. How do you answer her?
a: Refuse the port turn — slow down or turn to starboard
o: Agree — a VHF agreement replaces the Rules
Agree, and sound two short blasts as you turn
Ignore her — the Rules forbid passing deals by VHF
why: Rules 17(a)(ii) and 17(c): acting as stand-on, don't turn to port for a ship on your port side — a VHF deal doesn't override the Rules.

fig.title: Night, 4 M apart, closing
lines: Ship on your port bow, bearing steady
VHF: 'Motor yacht, I am keeping my
course — alter to port, green to green'

q: Both radar targets are closing. Which way may you turn to avoid them?
a: To starboard — away from both of them
o: To port — to pass astern of A
To port — but only once B has passed
Neither way — Rule 19 allows only slowing
why: Rule 19(d): no turn to port for A, forward of the beam, and none towards B, abaft it — a bold turn to starboard breaks neither.

fig.title: Fog · you 090°T, 8 kn
lines: A: 20° on your port bow, 3 M,
closing, CPA 0.2 M
B: on your port quarter, 1.5 M,
overtaking you, CPA 0.4 M

q: On watch in your 22 m motor yacht, you are coming up on these lights from astern at 6 kn more than her. What is she, and who keeps clear?
a: NUC and making way — you keep clear of her
o: Aground, with her anchor light — pass wide
NUC and stopped — the white is her anchor light
Fishing, not trawling — her gear is astern
why: Rule 27(a): two all-round reds; making way she adds sidelights and a sternlight — the one you see from astern. Rules 13 and 18: you keep clear.

fig.note: Night · fine ahead · radar: she makes 3 kn, you 9 kn

q: Your radar shows this vessel moving with exactly the set and rate of the current. She shows only these two reds. Is she lit correctly?
a: Yes — drifting, she makes no way through the water
o: No — she is moving, so she must show sidelights
No — two reds alone need an anchor light too
Yes — a NUC vessel never shows sidelights
why: Rule 27(a)(iii): NUC adds sidelights and a sternlight only when making way through the water — drifting with the stream, she isn't.

fig.note: Radar: she moves 070°T 2.0 kn · current 070°T 2.0 kn

q: Which day shapes does Rule 27 ask your yacht to hoist now?
a: Two black balls in a vertical line
o: One black ball where it can best be seen
Three black balls in a vertical line
Ball, diamond, ball in a vertical line
why: Rule 27(a)(ii): not under command — two balls in a vertical line; one ball means at anchor, three aground, ball-diamond-ball RAM.

fig.title: By day, 90 M offshore
lines: Your 22 m motor yacht: rudder jammed
You cannot steer or keep clear
Drifting, engines stopped

q: Motoring at night, you are catching up these lights from right astern. Can you tell from them whether the tow is over 200 m long?
a: No — from astern no masthead lights show
o: Yes — a tow over 200 m shows two yellows
Yes — the tow's diamond is lit at night
Yes — the tow then shows a second sternlight
why: Rule 24(a): the length shows in two or three masthead lights, seen from ahead and abeam; from astern, only the towing light and sternlights.

fig.note: Night · ahead, you catching up · radar: two echoes in line

q: This tug, towing a barge astern, is on your starboard bow at night. Which of the tug's own lights face you?
a: Her yellow towing light over her sternlight
o: Her masthead lights and her green sidelight
Her masthead lights and her red sidelight
Her white sternlight alone — no yellow
why: You bear 230°T from her, 130° from her bow — inside the 135° astern arc her sternlight shares with the yellow towing light above it.

fig.note: Night · she bears 050°T, heading 100°T, towing astern

q: Overtaking at night, you see these lights ahead; the low white on the left is the sternlight of her tow. What is she?
a: A tug whose tow severely restricts her turning
o: A tug towing a vessel not under command
A tug whose tow is over 200 m long
A pilot vessel towing a disabled yacht
why: Rule 27(c): a tow that severely restricts her from deviating from her course adds red-white-red to the 24(a) lights — yellow over the sternlight.

fig.note: Night · ahead, you are catching up

q: You are slowly catching up this dredger, working under way. On which side do you overtake her?
a: On your left — her port side, by the greens
o: On your right — her starboard side, by the reds
On either side — under way the pairs lapse
On neither — no one may overtake a RAM vessel
why: Rule 27(d): the greens mark the side to pass, the reds the obstruction — from astern her port side is on your left; Rule 13: you keep clear.

fig.note: Night · dredging under way · you are right astern

q: Motoring along the coast at 2200, you see these lights on a small boat 4 cables ahead, beside a charted dive site. What do you do?
a: Slow down and pass wide — divers may be down
o: Pass close — she is only a boat at anchor
Stand on — a small boat must keep clear of you
Stand by her — these are her distress lights
why: Rule 27(e)(i): a vessel too small for all the RAM lights shows red-white-red when diving — divers may be in the water round her.

fig.note: Night · a small boat, not moving, by a dive site

q: Your crew says the extra white light on this anchored buoy tender is a mistake. Are they right?
a: No — RAM at anchor adds her anchor light
o: Yes — at anchor the RAM lights replace it
Yes — a white there means she is making way
Yes — anchor lights are for ships over 50 m
why: Rule 27(b)(iv): a RAM vessel at anchor shows her anchor light as well; only dredging and underwater work (27(d)) drop it at anchor.

fig.note: Night · buoy tender at anchor, servicing a buoy

q: In a fishing fleet at night, you are 1 M astern of this vessel and closing. What is she doing?
a: Shooting her trawl — it is going out astern
o: Hauling her trawl — she is about to stop
Net fast on a wreck — she cannot move off
Towing another trawler a short way astern
why: Annex II 2(a)(i): two whites below the green-over-white trawling lights mean shooting nets — her trawl is paying out astern, towards you.

fig.note: 1 M ahead, in a fleet · lower pair seen from 1 M

q: Your track runs between these two vessels. What do you do?
a: Go round both — one net is towed between them
o: Pass between — 4 cables leaves you room
Pass close astern of the nearer — gear is ahead
Stand on — the searchlights mean they'll give way
why: Annex II 2(b): pair trawlers each direct a searchlight forward and towards the other — their net is strung between them: never pass between.

fig.title: Night, 1 M ahead
lines: Two vessels about 4 cables apart
Each: green over white, all round
Each shines a searchlight forward
and towards the other

q: On a night passage under power, this cluster of lights comes at you from right ahead at great speed. What is she, and what is your move?
a: A hovercraft head-on — alter to starboard
o: A WIG craft in flight — she keeps clear of you
A purse seiner — keep clear of her net
A vessel towing — the yellow shows her tow
why: Rule 23(b): an air-cushion vessel in the non-displacement mode adds an all-round flashing yellow; she is power-driven, so Rule 14 applies.

fig.note: Night · dead ahead, closing very fast

q: Your mate says this vessel must be 50 m or more, as she shows two masthead lights. Is he right?
a: Not necessarily — under 50 m she may show two
o: Yes — only ships of 50 m or more show two
Yes — under 50 m, two would mean towing
No — two masthead lights mean under 50 m
why: Rule 23(a)(ii): under 50 m a second masthead light is not required but allowed — and a tug's are in a vertical line, not like these.

fig.note: Night · 3 M off · no AIS

q: Which light falls short of Rule 22 for your length?
a: The masthead light — 5 M is needed from 20 m
o: The sidelights — 3 M is needed from 20 m
The sternlight — 3 M is needed from 20 m
The anchor light — 3 M is needed from 20 m
why: Rule 22(b): from 12 to 50 m a masthead light carries 5 M (only 3 M under 20 m); sidelights, sternlight and all-round lights 2 M.

fig.title: Survey of your 22 m motor yacht
lines: Masthead light: rated 3 M
Sidelights: rated 2 M each
Sternlight: rated 2 M
Anchor light: rated 2 M

q: How high and how far aft must that after masthead light be, at the least?
a: 11.0 m up, and 12 m abaft the forward one
o: 8.5 m up, and 12 m abaft the forward one
11.0 m up, and 6 m abaft the forward one
8.5 m up, and 6 m abaft the forward one
why: Annex I 2(a)(ii), 3(a): at least 4.5 m higher than the forward light (6.5 + 4.5 = 11.0 m) and half her length, 12 m, abaft it.

You choose to fit a second, after
masthead light, as ships do
Heights measured above the hull

q: Does this light meet the Rules for the Rule 34(b) light signals?
a: No — it must carry 5 M and sit 2 m clear of it
o: Yes — 2 M is the range for all-round lights
No — but only the range: 3 M is needed
No — but only the height: 4.5 m clear is needed
why: Rule 34(b)(iii) and Annex I 12: an all-round white seen at 5 M at least, 2 m or more vertically apart from a single masthead light.

lines: One masthead light, 7.0 m up
Offered: manoeuvring light, all-round
white, 2 M range, to go 1 m above it

q: Your crew hoists this small ball, bought for a dinghy. Does it meet Annex I for your yacht?
a: No — from 20 m a ball is at least 0.6 m across
o: Yes — any ball seen from 1 M will do
Yes — shape sizes apply only from 50 m
No — at anchor you show two balls, not one
why: Annex I 6: a ball is at least 0.6 m in diameter; only a vessel under 20 m may use smaller shapes to suit her size.

fig.note: Your 22 m motor yacht at anchor · ball 0.3 m across

q: At 0300 off the Breton coast you round these lights 1 M off, keeping them in view. From every side you see just these three. What is she?
a: Aground — her anchor light and two reds
o: Not under command, making way, seen from astern
Not under command and at anchor in the tide
At anchor and fishing, with her gear out
why: Rule 30(d): aground — anchor light(s) plus two all-round reds; a white seen from every side is all-round, not a 135° sternlight.

fig.note: Night · not moving · on a charted shoal

q: Which signals do the Rules ask of you until you float off?
a: Anchor light and two reds; bell with three strokes
o: Two reds only; one prolonged and two short
Anchor light only; the bell rung rapidly, 5 s
Two reds only; two prolonged blasts
why: Rules 30(d), 35(h): anchor light plus two all-round reds; the bell rung rapidly 5 s each minute, with three distinct strokes before and after.

fig.title: 0200, fog, your 22 m ketch aground
lines: On a sandbank, waiting for the flood
Aboard: bell, whistle, anchor light,
two all-round red lights

q: With the engines dead, which fog signal does Rule 35 ask of you now?
a: One prolonged and two short, every 2 min or less
o: Two prolonged, every 2 min or less — you're stopped
One prolonged, every 2 min or less — you're power
The bell, rung rapidly for 5 s every minute
why: Rule 35(c): NUC sounds one prolonged and two short, at most 2 min apart — the two prolonged of 35(b) is for a power vessel able to move.

fig.title: Fog, 90 M offshore, 0400
lines: Your 22 m motor yacht: both engines dead
Drifting, not under command
Two all-round reds shown

q: Creeping in at 3 kn, you hear this from the vessel ahead. What is she telling you?
a: She is at anchor and you are standing into her
o: She is aground and you are standing into danger
She is a pilot boat and wants you to stop
She is NUC and drifting down towards you
why: Rule 35(g): at anchor she rings the bell each minute and may add short-prolonged-short to warn an approaching vessel of her position.

fig.title: Fog, 0500, entering a roadstead
lines: Ahead, each minute: a bell rung
rapidly for about 5 s — and now also
short · prolonged · short

q: Which of these sound signals meets Annex III for your length?
a: B — 400 Hz, heard at 1 M
o: A — 150 Hz, heard at 2 M
C — 2,000 Hz, heard at 1 M
D — 400 Hz, heard at 0.5 M
why: Annex III: under 75 m the fundamental is 250–700 Hz; from 20 m the range is 1 M, set by tones up to 700 Hz — 2 kHz counts only under 20 m.

o: Yes — 110 dB at 1 m is all that is asked
Yes — any bell will do under 50 m
No — from 20 m you need a gong as well
why: Annex III 2: from 20 m the bell's mouth is at least 300 mm across and it gives 110 dB at 1 m; a gong is needed only from 100 m.

q: Is that sound signal right for a yacht under sail?

o: Yes — one short tells her you turn to starboard
Yes — any vessel in sight signals each turn
No — only the stand-on vessel may signal

o: The searchlight held on her bridge until she turns
The masthead strobe, flashing until she turns
A red flare — the signal ships notice most

o: A — the green star from the fishing boat
C — the strobe on the racing yacht
D — the searchlight swept over a sail
why: Annex IV 1(h): flames on the vessel, as from a burning tar or oil barrel, mean distress; green stars, strobes and searchlights do not.

B: flames from a barrel on a deck

q: What do you make of these bangs?

o: A warning — a firing range is active
A fog signal — she is at anchor
A salute — a warship is passing
why: Annex IV 1(a): a gun or other explosive signal fired at intervals of about a minute is a distress signal.

about once a minute for 10 min

q: Which yacht is NOT making an Annex IV distress signal?
a: B — the ensign flown upside down
o: A — the arms raised and lowered
C — the square flag and the ball
D — the orange smoke
why: Annex IV lists arms slowly raised and lowered, a square flag with a ball, orange smoke — an upside-down ensign is not among them.

Yacht B: her ensign flown upside down
Yacht C: a square flag with a ball below

q: What do the Rules say about your crew's plan?
a: No — a distress signal is for distress alone
o: Yes — out-of-date flares are no longer signals
Yes — if you tell the coastguard first
No — but hand flares are fine, rockets not
why: Annex IV 2: using or showing any distress signal except to indicate distress is prohibited — a red flare may start a search.
